subtopic_detail: Rash with fever and organ involvement six weeks after a new urate lowering drug
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar admitting a 62 year old man with a widespread rash, fever and malaise. He was started on allopurinol six weeks ago for recurrent gout and takes no other new medication.

He has a confluent morbilliform eruption over more than half his body surface with facial swelling, and there are no mucosal erosions and no skin detachment. His temperature is 38.7 degrees Celsius, pulse 102 beats per minute, blood pressure 122/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and SpO2 97 percent on room air. His white cell count is 16.8 x10^9/L with eosinophils 1.9 x10^9/L and atypical lymphocytes on the film, alanine aminotransferase is 312 units/L, creatinine 128 micromol/L and thyroid function is normal. He is of Han Chinese background.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 102 beats per minute, blood pressure 122/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 38.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Confluent morbilliform eruption over more than half the body surface, marked facial oedema, cervical lymphadenopathy, no mucosal erosions, no skin detachment
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 16.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0) with eosinophils 1.9 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5), atypical lymphocytes on film, alanine aminotransferase 312 units/L (5-35), creatinine 128 micromol/L (60-110)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue the allopurinol at a reduced dose and start systemic corticosteroid, with weekly monitoring of organ function
options.rationale: Continuing the culprit drug in any form perpetuates the reaction, and this drug has a long lived active metabolite so even a reduced dose maintains exposure. Complete withdrawal is the single most important intervention. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Cease the allopurinol and transfer him urgently to a burns unit for management of an epidermal necrolysis spectrum reaction
options.rationale: That spectrum is defined by mucosal erosions and epidermal detachment with a positive Nikolsky sign, and he has neither. The eosinophilia, facial oedema and six week latency point away from it towards a different severe reaction pattern. (Source: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions)
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions

options.text: Cease the allopurinol and give supportive care with emollients and antihistamines, avoiding systemic corticosteroid
options.rationale: Withdrawal alone is appropriate for a simple morbilliform drug eruption, but transaminases at nine times the upper limit with renal impairment place this in a different category. Undertreating visceral involvement is associated with progression and with a mortality around 10 percent. (Source: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions)
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions

options.text: Cease the allopurinol and start systemic corticosteroid, with weekly monitoring of liver and renal function
options.rationale: Eosinophilia, atypical lymphocytes, facial oedema, hepatitis and fever six weeks after starting the drug describe a drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms, where visceral involvement justifies systemic corticosteroid. Prolonged monitoring is needed because relapse and late thyroiditis are characteristic. (Source: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions)
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions

options.text: Cease the allopurinol and start intravenous immunoglobulin, with weekly monitoring of liver and renal function
options.rationale: Immunoglobulin has no established role in this reaction pattern and is expensive and volume loaded. It is considered in epidermal necrolysis and in refractory cases, not as first line for corticosteroid responsive visceral involvement. (Source: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions)
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions

explanation.summary: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms is a delayed hypersensitivity reaction with a characteristically long latency of two to eight weeks, which is why the culprit is often overlooked in favour of a more recently started medication. The classic features are an extensive morbilliform eruption, facial oedema, fever, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia or atypical lymphocytosis, and involvement of at least one internal organ, most often the liver. Allopurinol, aromatic anticonvulsants, sulfonamides, vancomycin and minocycline are the usual culprits in Australian practice. Treatment is immediate and permanent withdrawal of the drug, with systemic corticosteroid tapered slowly over six to twelve weeks when there is significant organ involvement. Two features distinguish it from other drug eruptions in follow up: symptoms can flare weeks after withdrawal as herpesviruses reactivate, and autoimmune sequelae such as thyroiditis and type 1 diabetes may appear months later, so monitoring continues well beyond recovery.
key_points: Latency of two to eight weeks distinguishes it from other drug eruptions
Eosinophilia or atypical lymphocytosis with organ involvement defines it
Allopurinol and aromatic anticonvulsants are the commonest culprits
Withdraw the drug permanently and treat organ involvement with corticosteroid
Monitor for late thyroiditis and other autoimmune sequelae for months
explanation.pearls: Consider testing for the HLA-B*58:01 allele before starting allopurinol in people of Han Chinese, Thai or Korean background, since carriage raises the risk of severe cutaneous reactions many fold, and always start at 50 to 100 mg daily with slow titration rather than at a dose chosen to reach target urate quickly.

sources.label: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions

subtopic_detail: Ketoacidosis after surgery in a patient whose glucose never rises above the usual diagnostic threshold
stem:
You are the medical registrar asked to review a 54 year old woman on the second day after an elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy. She has type 2 diabetes treated with metformin and empagliflozin, and she took her usual medications on the morning of surgery.

She is nauseated, breathing deeply at 28 breaths per minute, and complains of abdominal pain that the surgical team attributes to the operation. Her pulse is 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, SpO2 98 percent on room air and temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius. Her capillary glucose is 9.4 mmol/L. An arterial blood gas shows pH 7.21, bicarbonate 12 mmol/L, partial pressure of carbon dioxide 26 mmHg and lactate 1.4 mmol/L. Her sodium is 137 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, chloride 100 mmol/L and creatinine 88 micromol/L. Her wound sites are clean and her abdomen is soft.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Deep sighing respiration, dry mucous membranes, soft abdomen with mild port site tenderness, clean wounds
data_table.Investigations: Capillary glucose 9.4 mmol/L, arterial pH 7.21, bicarbonate 12 mmol/L (22-32), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 26 mmHg, lactate 1.4 mmol/L (0.5-2.0), sodium 137 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), chloride 100 mmol/L (95-110), creatinine 88 micromol/L (45-90)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Attribute the acidosis to metformin and give intravenous sodium bicarbonate while arranging urgent renal review
options.rationale: Metformin associated acidosis is a lactic acidosis and her lactate is 1.4 mmol/L with normal renal function, so the mechanism does not fit. Bicarbonate would mask the gap without addressing ongoing ketogenesis. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Attribute the picture to postoperative pain and nausea, give analgesia and an antiemetic, and repeat the gas in four hours
options.rationale: Deep sighing respiration with a pH of 7.21 is respiratory compensation for a metabolic acidosis, not a pain response, and four hours of observation allows the acidosis to deepen. The surgical attribution of her symptoms is the trap in this presentation. (Source: Australian Diabetes Society: Periprocedural diabetic ketoacidosis with SGLT2 inhibitor use)
source_refs: Australian Diabetes Society: Periprocedural diabetic ketoacidosis with SGLT2 inhibitor use

options.text: Measure blood ketones and start an intravenous insulin infusion with glucose and saline if they are raised
options.rationale: A high anion gap acidosis with a normal lactate and a glucose below the usual threshold in a patient on a sodium glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor is euglycaemic ketoacidosis until disproven. Insulin is required to switch off ketogenesis, and concurrent glucose is given because the blood sugar is already near normal. (Source: Australian Diabetes Society: Periprocedural diabetic ketoacidosis with SGLT2 inhibitor use)
source_refs: Australian Diabetes Society: Periprocedural diabetic ketoacidosis with SGLT2 inhibitor use

options.text: Attribute the acidosis to sepsis and start broad spectrum antibiotics with fluid resuscitation and blood cultures
options.rationale: She is afebrile with clean wounds, a normal lactate and a soft abdomen, none of which supports an infective source. Anchoring on sepsis delays the insulin that is the actual treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Restart her usual oral agents with intravenous fluid and recheck the gas once she is tolerating full oral intake
options.rationale: Continuing the cotransporter inhibitor sustains glycosuria and the ketogenic state that caused the problem, and oral agents cannot reverse an established ketoacidosis. The drug must be withheld until well after recovery. (Source: Australian Diabetes Society: Periprocedural diabetic ketoacidosis with SGLT2 inhibitor use)
source_refs: Australian Diabetes Society: Periprocedural diabetic ketoacidosis with SGLT2 inhibitor use

explanation.summary: Sodium glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors lower plasma glucose by causing glycosuria, which reduces insulin secretion and raises glucagon, shifting metabolism towards ketogenesis. Under the stress of surgery, fasting, dehydration or acute illness this can produce a full ketoacidosis while the plasma glucose remains below 14 mmol/L, so the diagnosis is missed if glucose is used as the screening variable. The clues are a high anion gap metabolic acidosis with a normal lactate, Kussmaul respiration, nausea and abdominal pain in a patient taking one of these drugs, and the confirmation is a raised blood ketone level. Treatment is an insulin infusion with concurrent intravenous glucose, since insulin is needed to suppress ketogenesis but the blood sugar cannot tolerate insulin alone, along with saline and potassium replacement. The Australian Diabetes Society advises withholding these drugs for at least two days before elective surgery, and the drug is not restarted until the patient is eating normally and the acidosis has fully resolved.
key_points: Ketoacidosis can occur with a glucose below 14 mmol/L on these drugs
A high anion gap with a normal lactate should prompt ketone measurement
Treat with insulin plus intravenous glucose, not insulin alone
Withhold the drug at least two days before elective surgery
Do not restart the drug until eating normally and fully recovered
explanation.pearls: Measure blood beta hydroxybutyrate rather than urine ketones, because the urine dipstick detects acetoacetate and reads falsely low early in ketoacidosis when beta hydroxybutyrate predominates, and can paradoxically appear to worsen during successful treatment as the ratio shifts back.

sources.label: Australian Diabetes Society: Periprocedural diabetic ketoacidosis with SGLT2 inhibitor use

subtopic_detail: Repeated explosive headaches in the weeks after childbirth with normal initial investigation
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 34 year old woman who is eleven days after an uncomplicated vaginal birth. She has had four separate headaches over six days, each reaching maximum intensity within a minute and each lasting about two hours, two of them triggered by coughing and one by showering.

Her pulse is 76 beats per minute, blood pressure 138/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent on room air and temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius. Non contrast computed tomography on day two of the headaches was normal, and lumbar puncture performed that day showed no xanthochromia and a normal cell count. Neurological examination is normal, the headache is not postural, and she has had no seizures. She has been using pseudoephedrine for nasal congestion and has no history of migraine.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76 beats per minute, blood pressure 138/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Normal fundi, no neck stiffness, no focal neurological deficit, normal visual fields to confrontation
data_table.Investigations: Non contrast computed tomography of the brain normal, cerebrospinal fluid with no xanthochromia and normal cell count, platelets 268 x10^9/L (150-400), urate and liver function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation and management?

options.text: Magnetic resonance venography with therapeutic anticoagulation started for a presumed cerebral venous thrombosis
options.rationale: Venous sinus thrombosis is an important postpartum diagnosis but typically produces a progressive headache over days with seizures, papilloedema or focal deficits rather than repeated discrete thunderclap events. Venography should be included in the imaging, but anticoagulation before a diagnosis is not justified. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Cerebral angiographic imaging with nimodipine started and the pseudoephedrine stopped
options.rationale: Recurrent thunderclap headaches over days, triggered by cough and bathing, in the postpartum period and with a vasoconstrictor on board describe reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome. Angiographic imaging demonstrates segmental narrowing, and management is removal of precipitants with calcium channel blockade. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Repeat computed tomography angiography with an epidural blood patch arranged for a presumed low pressure headache
options.rationale: Low cerebrospinal fluid pressure headache is postural, worsening within minutes of standing and relieved by lying flat, and hers is not. A blood patch for a non postural headache treats the wrong mechanism. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Catheter digital subtraction angiography with sumatriptan prescribed for the recurrent severe headaches
options.rationale: Triptans are vasoconstrictors and can precipitate stroke in this syndrome, so they are contraindicated even though the headache pattern may superficially suggest migraine. Catheter angiography is also rarely needed when non invasive imaging is available. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Repeat lumbar puncture with measurement of the opening pressure and acetazolamide started for raised pressure
options.rationale: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension causes a constant daily headache with visual obscurations and papilloedema, and her fundi and fields are normal. Repeating the tap adds risk without addressing the episodic explosive pattern. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: A thunderclap headache reaching peak intensity within a minute always requires exclusion of subarachnoid haemorrhage, and computed tomography within six hours followed by lumbar puncture for xanthochromia is the Australian pathway. When that pathway is negative and the headaches recur over days to weeks, reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome becomes the leading diagnosis. It is characteristically triggered by exertion, coughing, sexual activity or bathing, and the recognised precipitants are the postpartum state, serotonergic drugs, sympathomimetics including pseudoephedrine and cocaine, and immunoglobulin infusions. Angiographic imaging shows segmental beading of the intracranial arteries that resolves within three months, although it can be normal in the first week. Management is withdrawal of precipitants, nimodipine for symptom control, blood pressure control and strict avoidance of triptans and ergots, since the complications are convexity subarachnoid haemorrhage, ischaemic stroke and posterior reversible encephalopathy.
key_points: Exclude subarachnoid haemorrhage first with imaging and cerebrospinal fluid
Repeated thunderclap headaches over days point to vasoconstriction syndrome
Postpartum state and sympathomimetic drugs are the classic precipitants
Angiography may be normal in the first week and should be repeated if negative
Triptans and ergots are contraindicated because they worsen vasoconstriction
explanation.pearls: Ask what the patient was doing at the exact moment each headache began, because a syndrome in which every episode starts with coughing, straining, showering or orgasm is almost never migraine, and that single historical pattern separates this diagnosis from the far commoner postpartum headaches long before any imaging is arranged.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists: Headache

subtopic_detail: Choosing an anticoagulant class when the thrombosis accompanies an intact luminal bowel tumour
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 68 year old man with a newly diagnosed segmental pulmonary embolism found on a staging computed tomography scan. He has an untreated locally advanced rectal adenocarcinoma and is due to start chemoradiotherapy next week.

He is haemodynamically stable with a pulse of 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 128/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 percent on room air and temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius. Colonoscopy two weeks ago showed a friable circumferential tumour at 8 cm from the anal verge that bled on contact with the scope. His haemoglobin is 104 g/L, platelets 212 x10^9/L, creatinine 82 micromol/L and liver function tests are normal. He has been passing small amounts of fresh blood rectally most days for two months. He has no other anticoagulant indication.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 128/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Chest clear, calves soft, no abdominal mass palpable, digital examination confirms a firm rectal mass
data_table.Investigations: Computed tomography showing a segmental pulmonary embolism and a locally advanced rectal tumour, haemoglobin 104 g/L (130-170), platelets 212 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 82 micromol/L (60-110), liver function tests within normal limits

lead_in: Which anticoagulation strategy is most appropriate?

options.text: Warfarin with a target international normalised ratio of 2 to 3, continued while the cancer is active
options.rationale: Vitamin K antagonists perform poorly in cancer because appetite, vomiting, antibiotics and chemotherapy make control erratic, and the randomised evidence favours heparin over warfarin for recurrence. It is reserved for when neither preferred option is possible. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Insertion of a retrievable inferior vena cava filter without anticoagulation while he receives chemoradiotherapy
options.rationale: Filters are for patients in whom anticoagulation is absolutely contraindicated, and his bleeding is minor and from a tumour that treatment will shrink. They do not treat the existing clot and increase the rate of subsequent deep vein thrombosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Therapeutic low molecular weight heparin, continued for at least six months while the cancer is active
options.rationale: Rivaroxaban and edoxaban raise major gastrointestinal bleeding in patients with an intact luminal tumour, and this man is already bleeding from a friable rectal lesion. Low molecular weight heparin avoids that specific excess and remains the preferred option in this subgroup, continuing while the cancer is active. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Therapeutic rivaroxaban, continued for at least six months while the cancer is active
options.rationale: The randomised comparisons that established direct oral anticoagulants in cancer associated thrombosis showed their benefit was offset by major gastrointestinal bleeding concentrated in patients with luminal gastrointestinal tumours. He is the patient those trials warn about. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Observation with serial imaging and no anticoagulation, on the basis that the embolism was an incidental finding
options.rationale: Incidentally detected pulmonary embolism in cancer carries a recurrence and mortality risk comparable with symptomatic events, so it is treated the same way. Withholding treatment on the basis of how the clot was found is not supported. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Cancer raises the risk of venous thromboembolism several fold through tumour procoagulants, immobility, central venous access and chemotherapy, and the thrombosis is often found incidentally on staging imaging. Incidental events are treated as though they were symptomatic because their recurrence risk is comparable. Low molecular weight heparin was the standard for years on the basis of lower recurrence than warfarin, and direct oral anticoagulants have since been shown to be at least as effective, which makes them attractive for the avoidance of daily injections. The important exception is the patient with an intact luminal gastrointestinal or genitourinary tumour, in whom rivaroxaban and edoxaban produced a clear excess of major bleeding, so heparin or apixaban is preferred. Anticoagulation continues for at least six months and for as long as the cancer is active or treatment continues. Platelet count, renal function and the evolving bleeding risk are reviewed at every cycle.
key_points: Incidental pulmonary embolism in cancer is treated like a symptomatic event
Rivaroxaban and edoxaban increase bleeding with intact luminal tumours
Low molecular weight heparin is preferred in that specific subgroup
Warfarin performs poorly in cancer because control is erratic
Continue at least six months and while the cancer remains active
explanation.pearls: Reassess the choice after the tumour is resected or has responded, because the reason for choosing injections disappears with the friable lesion and many patients can then switch to an oral agent, which materially improves adherence over the years that anticoagulation may need to continue.

subtopic_detail: Proximal weakness that improves briefly with sustained effort in a long term smoker
stem:
You are the neurology registrar seeing a 64 year old man with five months of difficulty rising from low chairs and climbing stairs. He has smoked 45 pack years.

He describes a dry mouth, constipation and erectile difficulty over the same period. On examination proximal lower limb power is 4 out of 5, knee reflexes are absent at rest but become detectable after ten seconds of sustained quadriceps contraction, and grip strength improves briefly after repeated effort. There is no ptosis, no diplopia and no bulbar weakness. Creatine kinase is normal, inflammatory markers are normal, thyroid function is normal, and acetylcholine receptor antibodies are negative. A chest radiograph is reported as normal.

data_table.Examination: Proximal lower limb power 4 out of 5, absent knee reflexes that reappear after sustained contraction, dry mouth, no ptosis or diplopia, normal sensation
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 118 units/L (30-200), C reactive protein less than 5 mg/L, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, acetylcholine receptor antibodies negative, chest radiograph reported as normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Muscle biopsy of the vastus lateralis with myositis specific antibody testing for an inflammatory myopathy
options.rationale: An inflammatory myopathy would be expected to raise the creatine kinase and would not produce absent reflexes that reappear after exercise or autonomic symptoms. Biopsy would be invasive and uninformative here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Vitamin D and parathyroid hormone measurement with a trial of exercise for osteomalacic myopathy
options.rationale: Osteomalacic myopathy is a reasonable cause of proximal weakness but does not abolish reflexes, cause autonomic symptoms or show facilitation, and a normal alkaline phosphatase would be unusual. It does not account for the neurophysiological signature. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: A therapeutic trial of pyridostigmine with repeat acetylcholine receptor antibody testing in three months
options.rationale: Anticholinesterase treatment helps postsynaptic disease and is much less effective here, and the negative antibody with post exercise facilitation already points away from that diagnosis. Three months of trial delays the cancer search. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Computed tomography of the chest together with voltage gated calcium channel antibody testing
options.rationale: Post exercise facilitation of reflexes with autonomic features and proximal weakness describes a presynaptic neuromuscular junction disorder, which in a heavy smoker is associated with small cell lung cancer in around half of cases. A normal radiograph does not exclude a central tumour, so cross sectional imaging is required alongside the antibody. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbar spine with nerve conduction studies for a proximal radiculopathy
options.rationale: A radiculopathy produces sensory change in a root distribution and does not explain the dry mouth, constipation or the strengthening with repeated effort. The distribution here is symmetrical and not radicular. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Lambert Eaton myasthenic syndrome is caused by antibodies against presynaptic voltage gated calcium channels, which reduce the quantity of acetylcholine released at the neuromuscular junction and also impair autonomic cholinergic transmission. The clinical triad is proximal limb weakness worst in the legs, autonomic features such as dry mouth, constipation and impotence, and depressed or absent reflexes. The distinguishing sign is facilitation: both power and reflexes improve briefly after sustained or repeated contraction, the opposite of the fatigability seen in myasthenia gravis, and on nerve conduction studies this appears as a marked increment after brief exercise or high frequency stimulation. Around half of cases are paraneoplastic, almost always with small cell lung cancer, and the neurological syndrome commonly precedes the tumour by months to years, so a normal chest radiograph must be followed by computed tomography and by periodic re screening. Treatment addresses the tumour and uses amifampridine, with immunosuppression or immunoglobulin where needed.
key_points: Presynaptic calcium channel antibodies reduce acetylcholine release
Proximal weakness, autonomic features and absent reflexes form the triad
Post exercise facilitation distinguishes it from myasthenia gravis
Half of cases are paraneoplastic, almost always small cell lung cancer
A normal chest radiograph does not exclude a central tumour
explanation.pearls: Repeat the tumour search at intervals for two years even when the first computed tomography is clear, since the neurological syndrome can precede a detectable small cell lung cancer by that long, and positron emission tomography is the next step when conventional imaging remains negative in a heavy smoker.
